comments.text:
I have a very hard time trusting Teslas tech. There is just no redundancy, and even besides the associations to a man thats literally suing states for trying to outlaw AI generated child pr+n+graphy and interfering in elections across the world, there are just massive issues with the Move fast break stuff that all of Musks companies have. 

They have zero regards for peoples safety or existing regulatory frameworks or rules. And it shows. Here in Denmark, FSD-Supervised, now renamed to TAD, got launched in May and it has very frequent issues, driving onto bicycle lanes, down bus only roads, going the wrong way down one way streets, ignoring speed limits, being incapable of following its own route allignment, I could go on and on.

There is an interest in self driving cars where Im from in Denmark but we have no trials, no temporary permits, or anything like that. We do however have at least one company planning ahead. GreenMobility, which is actually a carsharing service rather than a ridehailing one, has signed a letter of intent for ordering Tensors for deployment in Denmark, getting priority in orders if they choose to excercise that option. But on the short term, theyve also announced a partnership with WeRide, a chinese autonomous car firm, with plans to deploy their vehicle, the WeRide GXR (a modified Farizon SV van with Lidars, cameras, and sensors, much like Waymos own approach) in the roads in 2027, hoping to get approval for level 4 operation in Greater Copenhagen.

Local governments in Denmark have also had an interest in autonomous EVs. Mainly as a last mile option in rural areas for public transit, replacing part of the current paratransit services and some infrequent rural bus lines. However that would likely have to wait for level 5 autonomy to become viable, cause while the cited statistics might be a tad outdated for now, they mentioned that to purchase and operate 5 autonomous EVs in a large geofenced rural area for 5 years would cost the same as operating 10 normal electric buses in the same timespan. So completely unfeasible economically for now.

I wont be denying that it could be a viable option down the road to implement self driving taxis on a greater scale, but it has to require that the equipment and operating expenses get cheaper, and that level 5 operation becomes possible, not to mention that whichever system does get permitted is safe and has redundancies.

comments.author: @florianjansen6216
comments.text:
A surprising number of factual errors for a Wendover documentary:

1. “Only running around 140 commercial robotaxis” — Tesla reported 300+ Cybercabs serving Austin alone on October 10. Texas records now list 1,080 registered Tesla robotaxis (although registered ≠ actively operating).
2. “Not providing services during evening and night hours” — Tesla already operated until midnight before this video. It now operates until 2 a.m. Tesla also reports 862,000 autonomous miles driven after dark.
3. “In early 2026 … hail a Cybercab” — Cybercab passenger service didn’t launch until September 3, 2026. Earlier rides used Model Ys.
4. “In 2022, the software was made available to all North American Tesla owners” — No. Only owners who purchased or subscribed to FSD could access it.
5. “Four to five million vehicles delivered with capable hardware … the fleet is already scaled” — Elon Musk himself admitted in April 2026 that HW3 cannot achieve unsupervised FSD without computer and camera upgrades.

These aren’t differences of opinion. They’re verifiable factual mistakes or misleading statements.

comments.author: @DotArve
comments.text:
"Ridesharing" like this is such a uniquely North American problem, and once they roll out will feel much like the  "we have ridesharing at home" meme.  I live in a Norwegian county slightly larger than all of Conneticut (or the greater metropolitan Seattle area)

We have an all-you-can eat, unlimited ride sharing in my county, with monthly prices varying between 16 and 66 USD.

It's just called "public transport" and in the areas where 90% of the people live, service is both frequent, close and flexible enough that using it should be the smart default.  In the largest urban area, pretty much nobody lives more than a five-minute very safe walk from the nearest bus stop.

Taxi service here?  That's for transportation of people with mobilithy or health issues … or drunk people
